Nomenclature description: A simple guide to the names, units and battery flows used on the home page, in power graphs and in the energy dashboard.
Nomenclature storage title: A battery changes when energy is used.
Nomenclature storage description: Charging keeps energy for later. Discharging releases it to power your appliances. The household total takes both directions into account.
Nomenclature diagram title: Electricity flows between solar panels, the grid, the battery and your home
Nomenclature diagram description: Solar panels supply electricity. The public grid supplies imports and receives exports. The battery stores electricity while charging and supplies it while discharging. The house uses the electricity left after charging and exports.
Nomenclature diagram note: Each arrow shows a possible direction. These flows do not all have to happen at the same time.
Nomenclature flows subtitle: Start with the direction: electricity coming in, going out or being stored.
Nomenclature grid description: Positive means you import electricity from the public grid. Negative means you export your surplus to it. This reading alone is not your whole household use.
Nomenclature solar description: The power produced by your panels. It can supply appliances, charge the battery or be exported to the grid.
Nomenclature battery description: Discharging supplies energy: add it. Charging stores energy: subtract it. Both readings are positive amounts; the formula gives them their signs.
Nomenclature house description: The power used by appliances, lighting and other household equipment. Energy being stored in the battery is left out of this total.
Nomenclature rule context: On the home page and in the power graphs, all the terms below are in watts (W). The grid term already includes exports as a negative value.
Nomenclature formula spoken: Household power equals net grid power plus solar power plus battery discharging power minus battery charging power.
Nomenclature formula explanation: Charging is subtracted because that electricity is being saved for later, rather than used by household appliances now. Battery discharge is added when that stored energy is released. If either battery flow is missing, the total uses only the grid balance and solar production.
Nomenclature example discharge title: Solar, grid and battery work together
Nomenclature example discharge descripti: You import 500 W, the panels produce 1,000 W and the battery supplies 300 W without charging. Your home uses 1,800 W.
Nomenclature example discharge spoken: 500 plus 1,000 plus 300 minus zero equals 1,800 watts.
Nomenclature example export title: Some energy is stored, some is exported
Nomenclature example export description: The panels produce 1,000 W. You export 200 W (grid: −200 W) and charge the battery at 300 W, with no discharge. Your home uses the remaining 500 W.
Nomenclature example export spoken: Minus 200 plus 1,000 plus zero minus 300 equals 500 watts.
Nomenclature units title: W and kWh: a moment or a period?
Nomenclature units subtitle: Power tells you how fast electricity is used. Energy tells you how much was used over time.
Nomenclature watts description: A reading at a particular moment. A 1,000 W heater uses electricity twice as fast as a 500 W heater while they are running.
Nomenclature kwh description: An amount accumulated over a period. The energy dashboard adds up the changing power readings across the selected hours or days.
Nomenclature unit example: 1,000 W running for 1 hour uses 1 kWh.
Nomenclature energy equation spoken: For constant power: multiply watts by hours, then divide by 1,000 to get kWh.
Nomenclature dashboard subtitle: These columns describe the selected period. All energy values are in kWh.
Nomenclature energy import: Electricity taken from the grid. Imports are counted as a positive amount, separately from exports.
Nomenclature energy solar: Electricity produced by the solar panels during the period.
Nomenclature energy discharge: Energy released from battery storage. A positive amount added to household use.
Nomenclature energy charge: Energy put into battery storage. A positive amount subtracted from household use.
Nomenclature energy total: Energy used by the household: grid imports + the displayed export value (already negative) + solar + battery discharge − battery charge. If either battery flow is unavailable, both battery terms are left out.
Nomenclature energy export: Surplus sent to the grid. This dashboard displays it as a negative number: −2 kWh means 2 kWh were exported.
Nomenclature energy saved: Total household energy minus grid imports. An estimate in kWh, not money saved or lower household use. Battery energy is included only when both charging and discharging data are available. It may have been stored in an earlier period or charged from the grid.
Nomenclature soc title: Battery level (%) is a different measure.
Nomenclature soc description: SOC means state of charge: how full the battery is. 60% describes its charge level, not a power in W or an energy in kWh.
Nomenclature unavailable description: Zero is a measured absence of flow. Unavailable means data is missing or incomplete. Without battery history, household totals use the grid balance plus solar production. Energy saved is calculated from that total. Battery columns remain unavailable. Grid and solar readings are still needed.
Nomenclature history description: Saved reports keep their recorded totals. If a total was left unavailable because battery data was missing, the display estimates it from the saved grid and solar values. The saved report itself is unchanged.
Nomenclature logic subtitle: How the app decides when to switch on devices, such as a water heater, using solar power that would otherwise go to the grid.
Nomenclature logic overview heading: Forcing first, then the battery, then each device in turn
Nomenclature logic overview text: Every second, the app reads the house meter and makes the same decisions, always in the same order.
Nomenclature logic step forced: A device forced by hand runs at its chosen level, whatever the battery does.
Nomenclature logic step battery: One yes-or-no answer for all the devices that are not forced. If the answer is no, they stay off.
Nomenclature logic step device a: The device with the highest priority takes what it needs from the surplus.
Nomenclature logic step device b: The next device gets what is left.
Nomenclature logic step more: Until every device has had its turn.
Nomenclature logic chart meter: Every second: read the house meter
Nomenclature logic chart forcing: Forced devices run at their chosen level
Nomenclature logic chart battery questio: Battery logic: may the other devices use the surplus?
Nomenclature logic battery intro: The battery is filled first. Devices may only use the power that the battery cannot take. This decision is the same for all devices that are not forced. Forcing is decided before it, so a forced device does not wait for the battery.
Nomenclature logic chart data available: Are the battery and meter readings available?
Nomenclature logic chart at max: Is it charging at its maximum power?
Nomenclature logic rule discharging why: The battery is already helping the house. A device would only empty it faster.
Nomenclature logic rule charging max: The battery is charging at its maximum power
Nomenclature logic rule charging max why: The battery cannot take more. The extra power would go to the grid, so a device may use it.
Nomenclature logic rule charging below: The battery is charging below its maximum power
Nomenclature logic rule charging below w: All the surplus still fits in the battery, so it goes there.
Nomenclature logic rule full: The battery is full and neither charging nor discharging
Nomenclature logic rule full why: The battery cannot store more, so the surplus may go to the devices.
Nomenclature logic rule other: The battery is not full and not charging
Nomenclature logic rule other why: There is no surplus for the battery, so there is none for the devices either.
Nomenclature logic rule missing: Readings are missing or too old
Nomenclature logic rule missing why: When the app is not sure, it plays safe and keeps the devices off.
Nomenclature logic check title: How the app checks the battery
Nomenclature logic max explanation: Zendure reports how much power goes into the battery. If it reaches the maximum charging power of the battery, the battery is charging at maximum. The 50 W margin is there because measurements are never perfectly exact.
Nomenclature logic full explanation: The battery is full when its level reaches the full level, 100 % by default.
Nomenclature logic independent: These checks only use what the battery reports. The devices play no part in them: the battery decision is made before the surplus is shared between the devices.
Nomenclature logic settings note: The maximum charging power and the full level are app settings. If no maximum charging power is set, the battery never counts as charging at maximum, so the devices wait until it is full.
Nomenclature logic examples intro: In these examples, no device is forced, and the battery can charge at up to 800 W, so “at maximum” means at least 750 W.
Nomenclature logic example morning title: Morning: the battery still has room
Nomenclature logic example morning descr: The battery is at 45 % and charges at 350 W. No device is running.
Nomenclature logic example midday title: Midday: the battery charges at full speed
Nomenclature logic example midday descri: The battery is at 70 % and charges at 800 W. The extra 600 W goes to the grid, so a device may use it.
Nomenclature logic example cloud descrip: The sun drops and the battery starts discharging 200 W to help the house. The devices switch off, even though the battery is at 90 %.
Nomenclature logic example full descript: The battery reaches 100 % and stops charging. It cannot store more, so the devices may use the surplus.
Nomenclature logic device intro: Each device is handled in turn, in priority order. Every device follows the same steps. A device forced by hand runs at its chosen level without waiting for the battery. The others also need the battery logic to say yes. Each device asks the app what to do every few seconds and follows the answer.
Nomenclature logic surplus explanation: P meter is the house meter reading. It is negative when power goes to the grid. P devices is the power of the automatic devices already running. The surplus is the power that would go to the grid if all these devices were off.
Nomenclature logic surplus example: Example: the meter shows −600 W while a water heater runs at 1,000 W.
Nomenclature logic chart device turn: Device X: its turn in the priority order
Nomenclature logic chart battery yes: Does the battery logic say yes?
Nomenclature logic chart contact: Has the device contacted the app recently?
Nomenclature logic chart forced level: Runs at the chosen level, whatever the battery does
Nomenclature logic chart next: Its power is taken from the surplus. The rest goes to the next device.
Nomenclature logic on off description: To switch on, the surplus must cover the whole power of the device. Once on, it stays on as long as the surplus stays above a small part of its power, for example 2 %. This stops it from switching on and off all the time.
Nomenclature logic on off equation: \begin{aligned} \text{Switch on if: } & \text{Surplus} > P_{\text{device}} \\ \text{Stay on if: } & \text{Surplus} > p \times P_{\text{device}} \end{aligned}
Nomenclature logic on off legend: P device is the power of the device. p is the small part, for example 2 %.
Nomenclature logic adjustable descriptio: The device runs at a level between 0 % and 100 % that follows the surplus. A small part is kept aside, as for on/off devices. Some devices also have a top level that they never go above.
Nomenclature logic adjustable legend: The level is kept between 0 % and 100 %.
Nomenclature logic priority title: Sharing the surplus between two devices
Nomenclature logic priority description: The surplus is 2,500 W. Device A has priority 1: it is on/off and uses 2,000 W. Device B has priority 2: it is adjustable up to 1,000 W, with 2 % kept aside (20 W).
Nomenclature logic priority a descriptio: The surplus covers its whole power, so it switches on. 500 W are left for the next device.
Nomenclature logic priority b descriptio: It only sees the 500 W that device A left. After keeping 20 W aside, it runs at 48 %.
Nomenclature logic limits title: When a device stays off anyway
Nomenclature logic limit target descript: Some devices send a measurement, such as the water temperature. When it goes above the target, the device stops. It can only start again once a waiting time, for example 15 minutes, has passed without reaching the target.
Nomenclature logic limit energy descript: A device can have an energy limit over a period, for example 6 kWh over the last 4 hours. Once it is reached, the device stays off.
Nomenclature logic limit forced descript: A device can be forced to a chosen level. It then ignores the surplus and the battery logic, but the limits above still apply. It also stops while the house meter cannot be read.
Nomenclature logic limit contact descrip: A device that has not contacted the app for a while is treated as off. Its power is no longer counted.
Config sign in: Sign in to edit the configuration
Config email note: Only allowed email addresses receive a login code.
Config note: Allowed emails apply as soon as they are saved; other settings need a restart.
Config restart required: Saved settings differ from the running ones. Restart to apply them.
Config code sent: If {email} is allowed, a code valid for {minutes} minutes has been sent to it.
Config saved: Saved. A backup of the previous version is in config.json.bak.
Config restart timeout: The server did not come back after one minute. Check its logs.
Config session expired: Your session has expired. Please sign in again.
Config request failed: The request failed. Check the connection and try again.
Config error code-expired: Code expired. Request a new one.
Config error too-many-attempts: Too many attempts. Request a new code.
Config error mails-required: At least one allowed email (auth.mails) is required.
Config error config-object: The configuration must be a JSON object.
Config error write-failed: config.json could not be written. Check the server logs.
Config error read-failed: config.json could not be read. Check the server logs.
Config sender setup note: No account is configured yet to email the login codes. Enter a Gmail address and one of its app passwords (Google account › Security › App passwords). They are saved to config.json once you have signed in with the code sent through them.
Config error sender-required: Enter the sender address and its app password.
Config error sender-failed: The sender could not sign in to the mail server:
Self-sufficiency hint: Share of the household use not bought from the grid
Self-consumption hint: Share of the solar energy used at home or stored instead of exported
Energy flow note: Estimated from the day totals: grid export and battery charging are counted as solar first.
House supplied by: Where the household energy came from
Power since midnight note: 5-minute averages. Grid: import above zero, export below. Battery: discharging above zero, charging below.
Hourly energy note: Sources above zero, grid export and battery charging below (lighter, outlined). The line is the household use.
